hints.S57_A1: The dash spells it out: EASY TO UNDERSTAND and PERFECTLY TRANSPARENT, like A GLASS OF WATER. Ask: which word describes an explanation you can see straight through? 'Heavy', 'cold' and 'slow' say nothing about understanding.
hints.S57_A2: She DRAGGED HERSELF to the lab, so she was certainly not feeling good that morning. Ask: which idiom means feeling unwell? 'Excited', 'on top of the world' and 'over the moon' all describe someone who feels wonderful.
hints.S57_A3: The club wants TO TEST WHETHER PLANTS GROW FASTER with music, so the work must actually be done. Ask: which phrasal verb means to perform a task from start to finish? 'Stop' and 'give up' cancel it; 'look after' means care for.
hints.S57_A4: He wrote down THE TIME, TEMPERATURE AND RESULTS FOR EACH TRIAL - a running record, kept in order. Ask: which book is made for recording data? A storybook and a novel are invented, and a poster is for display.
hints.S57_A5: The mixture BUBBLED, HISSED AND GAVE OFF HEAT the moment the ACID TOUCHED THE METAL. Ask: which word names what happens when two substances meet and change each other? A smell or a weight cannot 'take place'.
hints.S57_B1: The subject is NOBODY, not the science class around it. Words like nobody and everyone count as ONE person, however many faces you picture. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb or the one wearing -s?
hints.S57_B2: 'HAS' is waiting for its partner, and the prize was taken TWO YEARS IN A ROW. Ask: after 'has', which form builds the present perfect - the plain one, the -s one, the -ing one, or the past participle? This verb is irregular.
hints.S57_B3: THAN sets GROUP A against Group B - two things only - and the adjective has three syllables. Ask: can a long adjective ever take -er, or does it need a helper word in front? 'Most' belongs with three or several things, and an -ly word would describe a verb.
hints.S57_B4: The FIRE ALARM INTERRUPTED the lesson - it cut across something already under way. Ask: which choice shows an action still going on in the PAST? A plain past verb reports a finished action, not one caught in the middle.
hints.S57_B5: EQUIPMENT cannot be counted - you never say 'one equipment, two equipments'. Ask: which choice partners an uncountable noun? 'Few', 'a few' and 'many' all need things you can count one by one.
hints.S57_B6: The SCIENCE FAIR statement is positive, and its verb is a form of 'to be' set in the past. Ask: does a tag echo the verb already in the sentence, or borrow 'did'? And does a positive statement take a positive tag or a negative one?
hints.S57_B7: The RESULTS did not do the checking - THE TEACHER did, and it happened before the other classes saw them. Ask: which choice is passive (the subject receives the action) and set in the past? 'Results' is plural, so pick the plural helper.
hints.S57_B8: ASKED THE STUDENTS = a reported request, and the data must reach the SHARED FOLDER. Ask: after 'asked + person', which form comes next - the plain verb, the -ing form, or 'to' + verb? Pick the full infinitive.
hints.S57_C1: The passage calls them RULES and adds WITHOUT EXCEPTION - there are NO EXCUSES. Ask: which box word is the strongest obligation, the one that leaves no choice at all? 'Ought to' is only advice, and advice can be ignored.
hints.S57_C2: Read the condition: ONLY IF THE TEACHER GIVES YOU A PASS. Leaving early is not a duty - it is something you are allowed to do. Ask: which box word grants permission instead of forcing an action?
hints.S57_C3: NOBODY WILL PUNISH YOU FOR FORGETTING, yet labelling samples is SIMPLY GOOD PRACTICE. Ask: which box phrase gives advice about the right thing to do, with no penalty attached? A rule word would be far too strong here.
hints.S57_C4: Look at the word already printed in front of the blank: WILL. Ask: which box phrase can follow 'will' and still mean an obligation? Two modal words can never stand side by side - say each choice aloud after 'will' and listen.
hints.S57_C5: WITH ENOUGH PRACTICE, the pupil manages it WITHOUT ANY HELP AT ALL - the sentence describes skill, not duty. Ask: which box phrase names what a person has learned to do? One pupil, so watch the singular form.
hints.S57_C6: ONLY ONE MICROSCOPE then, BUT NOW THERE ARE EIGHT: the sentence sets a past situation against today's. Ask: which box phrase describes something that was true in the past but has since changed?
hints.S57_C7: The warning comes after the comma: OR THE TEACHER WILL NOT ACCEPT YOUR REPORT. Ask: which box phrase gives strong advice with a threat hidden inside it? A permission word carries no consequence whatsoever.
hints.S57_C8: The word THAN near the end is the giveaway: two activities are being weighed against each other. Ask: which box phrase means 'prefer one thing to another' and needs THAN to finish it off?
hints.S57_D1: The dash defines it: A PREDICTION ABOUT WHAT WILL HAPPEN, formed FIRST, before any testing. Ask: which box word names a scientist's careful guess? The test itself comes afterwards, to check it.
hints.S57_D2: 'AN' in front of the blank means the word starts with a vowel sound, and its purpose is TO TEST THIS PREDICTION. Ask: which box word names the test itself, the thing scientists DESIGN AND CONDUCT?
hints.S57_D3: DURING THE TEST they watch and NOTE EVERY DETAIL. The blank follows 'carefully', so it must be a verb. Ask: which box word means to watch closely and notice what is happening? A noun cannot fit here.
hints.S57_D4: The example after the dash gives it away: FOR EXAMPLE, ONLY THE TEMPERATURE, WHILE KEEPING EVERYTHING ELSE THE SAME. Ask: which box word names one condition that may be changed in a fair test?
hints.S57_D5: AT THE END the scientist explains WHAT THE RESULTS SHOW and whether the prediction was correct. Ask: which box word names the final judgement, written only after all the evidence is in?
hints.S57_E1: Read the subject aloud: THE RESULTS - one table can hold many of them. Ask: is the underlined verb singular or plural, and which does a plural subject demand? Never match a verb to the noun that happens to sit nearest.
hints.S57_E2: 'WEAR' is what you do with clothes, but this sentence points to A ROOM - a place with LARGE WINDOWS. Ask: which spelling means 'at which place'? Two words can sound alike and still mean entirely different things.
hints.S57_E3: 'YEILD' puts the E in front of the I. Ask: in this word, which letter really comes first? Remember: I before E, except after C - the same order as in shield, belief and niece.
hints.S57_E4: The underlined word tells us HOW the student MEASURED the plant, so it describes the action, not the student. Ask: does an action verb take an adjective or an adverb after it? Adverbs of manner usually end in -ly.
hints.S57_E5: The OBSERVATIONS belong to the GROUPS - several groups, each with its own notes. Ask: does a bare -s ever show ownership? When the owner word already ends in -s, only one mark of punctuation is missing, and it goes after the -s.
hints.S57_F1: 'ALTHOUGH' already carries the contrast, so the two halves must not fight twice. Ask: if 'although' opens the sentence, may you still drop 'but' into the middle? Decide which half is the surprise before you write.
hints.S57_F2: Sentence B still wears its question clothes: 'WHAT DOES THE EXPERIMENT SHOW?' Ask: once it is reported, does the helper 'does' survive? And which tense does the verb slide into after the word 'asked'?
